According to the Rav, rain is a bad sign only on the first night of Sukkos, because only then is there an obligation to eat in the sukkah; on other days a person has a choice.
The mitzvah of sukkah is to dwell there; like an address, the sukkah stays one's home even when rain sends him out.
The kezayis eaten on the first night establishes the sukkah as one's dwelling for all seven days, a stronger fixing than the meal placed for an eruv.
The creation of Chava and her coming to Adam repeats every year between Hashem and Knesses Yisrael, from Rosh Hashanah to Shemini Atzeres.
Nisuin is a closer bond than erusin, yet its punishment is lighter, because it comes from the attribute of chesed.
The rain on Sukkos is the Satan's share at a time of great holiness, and a sign that a year of union with Hashem is approaching.
The breaking of the luchos is joined to Bereishis: after a broken Sukkos one can begin again.
The Rav reads the Rambam's limit as a matter of choice: a bad sign is only where a person had no choice, and only the first night of Sukkos obliges him to eat in the sukkah.
Leaving the sukkah for rain does not end one's dwelling there, just as a man's home address does not change when he steps out; therefore the exemption of one who suffers fits the mitzvah of dwelling.
An eruv is fixed for one day by placing a meal, but the sukkah must be fixed as a home for seven days, which needs an actual eating on the first night; this is why the kezayis is learned from matzah.

Tishrei is the yearly rebuilding of Chava for Adam: Rosh Hashanah as back to back, the shofar breaking through judgment, Yom Kippur as the separation, the sukkah as chuppah, and Shemini Atzeres as 'He brought her to the man'.
The Rav applies the Ramban's rule, that what comes from love carries a lighter punishment, to explain why a nesuah is punished by strangling while an arusah is stoned.
The missing heh in the Torah's word for a young woman points to what she lacks until nisuin, when she receives the heh and is raised to be one with her husband.
The breaking of the luchos at the end of the Torah is joined to its first word, Bereishis, which holds everything like a seed; so a broken Sukkos becomes a new beginning.

Why must one eat a kezayis in the sukkah on the first night?
Why is the nesuah, more closely bound to her husband, punished more lightly than the arusah?

Adam found his ezer only after his own search through all the animals failed and Hashem cast sleep on him: real help comes from Hashem, not from one's own running.
The sukkah is the shelter of bitachon, the mark of Yaakov Avinu, the father of bitachon, and from Sukkos one takes bitachon for the whole year.
The Rav raises Rashi's question why the Torah does not begin with the first mitzvah, and Rashi's answer that the nations should not be able to call the Jews robbers.
The Torah contains three Torahs: the Torah of creation, the Torah of man given to the nations, and the Torah of Yisrael.
Creation was put under the control of man; when man keeps his Torah, nature keeps its Torah, and after three failures Hashem gave the keys to Avraham and his children.
Eretz Yisrael is the center and foundation of creation, which is why all the nations want a share in it.
All of Bereishis is an introduction to 'Hachodesh hazeh lachem', explaining why the Torah of Yisrael was given only to the Jews.

Since the Torah is the blueprint of the world, the first time a thing appears in it defines it; the first 'ezer', Chava, was given to Adam only after all his efforts failed and he slept, so help by its nature comes without human action, an exercise in bitul.

The Gemara's laws of sukkah focus on sleeping rather than eating, because sleep is the essence of the sukkah: only one who feels secure can sleep, and the sukkah is a flimsy hut under Hashem's protection.
Nature is itself a Torah: a bird flying fulfills a command of the Torah just as a Jew putting on tefillin does, the only difference being that man has free choice.

Because nature is written in the Torah, a miracle that changes nature changes the Torah, which is why the Gemara criticizes the man for whom nature was changed and why tzaddikim avoided making miracles.

Creation keeps its Torah only when man keeps his: in the generation of the flood even the animals strayed from their kinds, while in the generation of the desert nature flourished so that one cluster of grapes needed eight men.

Bereishis is a history of three strikes against mankind, Adam, the flood and the dispersion, after which the keys of creation passed to Avraham, and even then the nations were given a last chance at Sinai.

The nations' claim to Eretz Yisrael, unlike any other land taken by conquest, comes from its being the center and root of creation, which even its name, the Mediterranean, 'middle of the land', reflects.

Why does the Gemara criticize a man for whom a miracle was made?
Why does the Torah begin with Bereishis and not with the first mitzvah given to Yisrael?

Chanukah's light on the darkest night
The weekly parsha is connected to the matters of its week, and Vayeshev and Miketz carry themes connected to Chanukah.
The light of Chanukah, brought down through the mesirus nefesh of the Chashmonaim, can kindle even souls that Shabbos cannot kindle.
Citing the Kad HaKemach, the Rav says that while the Chanukah lights burn, the hidden light, the light of Mashiach, is revealed in them.

The parsha of Yehuda and Tamar holds the birth of Mashiach ben David through Peretz, and the parsha of Yosef and Potiphar's wife leads to Mashiach ben Yosef through Asenath and Ephraim, so both Mashiachs are found in this sidra.
Hashem steers history in two ways: sometimes salvation comes through the good deeds of tzaddikim, and sometimes through the acts of the wicked, who are unknowing tools of His plan.
Yosef refused Potiphar's wife even though she argued that Mashiach would come from them, holding that one may not bring Mashiach through an aveirah.
Chanukah usually falls near the tekufah, the longest night, and on that darkest night the Jews kindle the light of Mashiach.

The wicks and oils that may not be lit on Shabbos but may be lit on Chanukah stand for souls that Shabbos cannot kindle, while the light of Chanukah, drawn down by the Chashmonaim's mesirus nefesh, can.
Although the Shechinah never descended below ten tefachim, the Chanukah lamp is placed below ten, because on Chanukah the Shechinah comes down to those lying low who have no strength to rise.
Both parshiyos open with a descent, Yehuda's going down and Yosef's being brought down, hinting that the light of both Mashiachs comes down to the heel, the lowest generation.
Potiphar's wife's intention for Heaven was flawed: Tamar was ready to be burned rather than shame Yehuda, but Potiphar's wife, whose intention was mixed with desire, had Yosef thrown into prison.
Rashi notes that the day was the Egyptians' festival because on that day, the tekufah, Torah is not learned, so Yosef lacked the protection from impure thoughts that, per the Rambam, Torah gives.

The sitra achra always imitates kedushah: as the Jews light up the darkest nights on the 25th of Kislev, the nations darken the 25th of their month with their lights, the opposite of the light revealed on Chanukah.

The brachah goes over the more important food because holding it in hand awakens a greater feeling of thanks to Hashem.
Hashem's Name is Shalom and rests only on what is whole, which is why a blemished kohen or korban is unfit for the avodah.
Every Jew must eventually reach Olam Haba, because every Jewish soul comes from there; mitzvos and sins only make the road easier or harder.
Shabbos, Torah, Eretz Yisrael and Olam Haba are one thing, and the Jewish people is rooted in all of them.
A Jew is Hashem's child and can never stop being His child; sins bring punishment but do not undo the relationship.
The days of Sefirah are days of battle, in which a Jew must prepare himself for Shavuos by refining his seven middos.

The rule of making the brachah over the more important food is not about valuing quality for its own sake, but because the more important food awakens a stronger feeling of thanks, which is the point of a brachah.

The advantage of a whole loaf is of a different kind: not gratitude but shleimus, on which Hashem's Name rests, as learned from the kohen and korban with a blemish; this is why Rabbi Yochanan uses a different wording from Rav Huna.

Jews do not gain their bond to Olam Haba, Torah and Eretz Yisrael through mitzvos; the reverse is true: because they are bound to them, they were given mitzvos. This is why the Torah opens with Bereishis rather than the first mitzvah.

Just as a Jew and a non-Jew, and Shabbos and the weekdays, are different in kind, Eretz Yisrael is the 'Jewish land' whose inner essence is Torah and Shabbos; therefore it too keeps Shabbos, and its Yovel parallels Yom Kippur, the Shabbos of Shabbos.

The seven nations of Canaan are the seven middos; conquering the land means refining one's own middos during the seven weeks of Sefirah, until even the weekdays become 'Jewish' and everything is drawn into Shabbos.
The shedim were left without bodies not for lack of time but because they were created lacking shleimus, so that they could have no connection to Shabbos, which is wholeness.

Why does the Mishnah 'Kol Yisrael' come right after the laws of those liable to death by beis din?
Why does the Torah begin with Bereishis and not with the first mitzvah?

The Rav says one must love what should be loved: Hashem, the Torah and a fellow Jew, and give all seven middos over to Hashem.

Moshe Rabbeinu's prayers in Va'eschanan teach that one first sets out the praise of Hashem and only afterwards prays.
Korbanos and pesukei dezimra cut a path through the forces that block tefillah, like an army breaking through enemy positions.
Pesukei dezimra is not a lesser part of davening: the less obligatory a thing is, the dearer it is to Hashem.
One should daven together with the tzibbur, come on time and keep pace with the chazzan, and one owes the tzibbur a lively davening that arouses others.
Tefillah requires toil just as Torah does; davening with warmth and a raised voice breaks through the coarseness of the body.
The 'uncle' who talks a Jew out of a good deed is the yetzer hara in disguise, and one must recognize him.
Pesukei dezimra 'cut through' (zemer meaning to cut) the forces that block prayer; it is the war of David, the warrior king, waged with his songs.
The less obligatory a thing is, the dearer it is to Hashem; doing what one need not do shows greater devotion.
In Hallel Hagadol each angel can say only one praise, while a Jew who says them all includes the whole row of angels.
On weekdays the alphabetic blessing has a word per letter, on Shabbos a whole phrase per letter, because Shabbos's added holiness spreads into whole phrases of song.
A person's soul is scattered in many places, and he is led to a place to gather its parts and redeem the souls found there.
When a person is attacked by doubts about a good deed, it is a sign he carries something precious, as robbers ambush only the truck with money.
The first thought on waking to get up and serve Hashem comes from the soul; the second, which talks one out of it, is only a reaction of imagination.

He asks that people come to davening on time and daven together with the chazzan, not lagging behind.

Hashem ordered the world as giver and receiver: the lesser receives from the greater by bowing to him, and so a Jew needs a rebbe to receive yiras Shamayim.
Malchus, the trait of Dovid HaMelech, is having nothing of one's own, like the moon that only receives the sun's light; Shabbos and Yerushalayim share this quality.
On the Regalim Jews go up to the place of malchus, but on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur the King comes to them.
The Torah's king exists to teach the people that they and the world are nothing and only Hashem is, so that through him they choose Hashem.
Kings of Dovid's house may sit in the Azarah because they are so batel to the Mikdash that they become part of its building.
Being 'tamim' with Hashem means not searching out the future and knowing that everything is run by Hashem alone; this is bitachon.
One is batel to the kohen because the kohen stands batel before Hashem; this is why the law of standing in service is stated in the parsha of the kohanim's gifts.

Malki-Tzedek's blessing of Avraham before Hashem, for which he lost the kehunah, is read by the Rav as also an acknowledgment that Avraham was greater, through whom he could reach a higher bittul to Hashem.
Yerushalayim is the Shabbos of the world: like Shabbos, it produces nothing of its own, and for that very reason it is the source of blessing.
The miracle that the people stood crowded yet bowed with room is explained by bittul: one who is batel to Hashem takes up no space.

A king of Dovid's house may sit in the Azarah because his complete bittul makes him part of the building itself, like its stones and wood; this also explains why Dovid is mentioned right before the closing of Boneh Yerushalayim.
In Avraham's war with the kings, throwing dust was not a lack of trust but an expression of bittul: before Hashem the kings were nothing, like dust.
The law that the avodah is done standing appears among the people's duties to the kohen because the kohen's standing bittul is the very reason one is batel to him.
Why is the law that the avodah is done standing stated here, among what the people owe the kohen, and not in Vayikra with the laws of the avodah?
Why is there no mitzvah of aliyah l'regel on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur?
Why did Avraham throw dust at the kings, if he trusted that Hashem would help?
Why may kings of Dovid's house sit in the Azarah, where no one else may sit?
How can the brachah of Boneh Yerushalayim mention Dovid right before its closing, when the words before the closing must match it?

Haazinu contains the whole Torah and everything that will happen, which is why it is read in the days that, like Rosh Hashanah, contain the whole year.
According to the Ramban, Haazinu promises the redemption without any condition of teshuvah, and everything it foretells has come true.
Haazinu is a song because emunah shows that everything, even what is bitter, comes from Hashem, and so it cannot be bad.
The success of the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah depends on davening with emunah, as if one saw the Judge writing the year's decree.
Not answering amen is a lack of emunah that prolongs the galus, which explains the severe language about talking during chazaras hashatz.
Rosh Hashanah is a day of gathering: all days gather to their head and all souls to their root, and each Jew must reach the innermost point of yechidah.
A Jew who makes Hashem King over all his thoughts, words and deeds is the switch that reveals Hashem's kingship over the whole world.

The Rav reads 'Rosh' Hashanah like the first letter of a word, which already holds the whole word in potential: the whole year is contained in Rosh Hashanah, and in the same way Haazinu contains the whole Torah.
Haazinu itself answers the question of why the Jews of Europe did not resist: one could chase a thousand only because Hashem had handed them over, and Haazinu foretold it.
Jews rejoice in the Day of Judgment because they want to be judged by Hashem Himself, like a child who runs to his mother even knowing she may slap him.
What comes from Hashem can be bitter but never bad, like a bitter wine that is in fact excellent, as only a connoisseur knows.
The hundred sounds of the shofar correspond to the ten utterances of creation, each including ten, so that hearing the shofar is like standing at the root of the year's whole course.

Malchiyos opens with Aleinu because Yehoshua said it when he broke through the walls of Yericho: accepting Hashem's kingship means breaking the wall around one's own heart to reach the point of yechidah.
Rebbi's suffering for the calf was not a punishment that Yom Kippur could atone for, but a reality: Hashem's mercy toward a person follows that person's own mercy.

The Rav says one must daven in the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah with true emunah, as if seeing with one's own eyes how the year is being decided.
The Rav urges listening to every brachah of the chazzan and answering amen, and not talking during chazaras hashatz.
The Rav says one must make Hashem King over all of one's desires, thoughts, words and deeds.
The Rav says that in the days of judgment one must not forget for a minute to daven with mercy for the Jewish people and Eretz Yisrael.

The forty days of Elul were days of favor, and the teshuvah Klal Yisrael did then left a lasting mark on the season for all generations.
Shmitah means letting go; when a person releases what others owe him, Hashem correspondingly releases the debt of his sins.
Elul calls for strengthening one another in serving Hashem, and letzanus is what most cools a person's Yiddishkeit.
Following Rabbi Tzadok, emunah is the root and entrance of all good and letzanus is the root of all bad and the entrance to the opposite.
A scoffer is pushed away from the palaces of tefillah and loses his connection to davening and learning.
Pharaoh withstood the plagues because, as a scoffer, he used jokes to escape reality, and Hashem punished him measure for measure by making sport of Egypt.
The Rav reads 'shmitah to Hashem' as a mirror: by letting go of the debts others owe us, we cause Hashem to let go of the debt our sins have created.
Because the shmitah of years is counted from Tishrei, Rosh Hashanah is itself a time of release, and every Shabbos, the seventh day, is a small Rosh Hashanah with the same power.
Letzanus is the exact opposite of emunah: emunah is the gate into serving Hashem, and letzanus is the gate out of it.

Following Rabbi Tzadok, the Gemara's statement that scoffers do not receive the Shechinah means that the scoffer is kept out of the palaces of tefillah, so that even while davening his mind wanders elsewhere.
Pharaoh's superhuman stubbornness through the plagues came from his humor: a joke lets a person escape reality, so he never has to face it.
Pharaoh's punishment, 'that I made sport of Egypt', was measure for measure: Hashem let him make good jokes and then made a joke of him.

The Rav says that the davening of this time should begin by accepting the mitzvah of loving one's fellow as oneself.
The Rav says one must strengthen others in serving Hashem and never cool them off with scoffing.

Elul is a city of refuge, and like the Torah's signs at the crossroads it must be pointed out so that people actually flee into it.
The Arizal's promise for saying L'Dovid Hashem Ori is fulfilled only when one takes its message of bitachon to heart, as with the Gemara's promise for Ashrei.
Bitachon decides practical conduct: coming to shul, guarding the eyes, not talking before davening or in the mikveh, and not interrupting learning for news.
The forty days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Yom Kippur are a mikveh of forty se'ah, and each of their 960 hours is one lug.
Elul calls above all for teshuvah on middos and bein adam lachaveiro, since shaming another is a form of shedding blood.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's teaching that Yom Kippur does not atone for sins against another points at what must be fixed, which is why Ne'ilah focuses on the wrong done to others.
Just as the Torah was not satisfied with building cities of refuge but demanded signs at every crossroads, Elul does not help on its own: it must be announced and pointed out, or people pass it by.
Elul's verse, 'a road in the sea', describes a path that does not hold still: without constant signposts one drifts, and the forty days are gone before one notices.
One who truly relies only on Hashem is judged by Hashem alone and not by the lower courts, which explains the Arizal's promise that the sayer of L'Dovid emerges meritorious.
Following Rashi, the heart's stirring in Elul is itself Hashem's message, delivered through the heart as His messenger, telling a Jew to seek Him.

Every hour of the forty days is one lug of a mikveh; wasted hours are like drawn water poured in, and the remedy is to join oneself to Hashem, the true tzaddik, as a mikveh is repaired through contact with a kosher one.

Torah's inability to make miracles beyond nature comes from its greatness, not its weakness: nature is the Torah's own law, and a tzaddik who changes the order of Creation is in effect changing the Torah.

The oil that held for eight days was the same kind of miracle as the few defeating the many, so the lights served as a mirror in which the hidden miracle of the war could be seen.

The first se'ir of Rosh Chodesh, at the dedication of the Mishkan, was not eaten because on that day the moon was not diminished, and this is the best sign for all generations.
Every sin grows from a bad midda; whoever repents only for the sin and not for the midda falls back into the same sin.
In Nissan and Sefirah one repairs the middos, the root; in Tishrei the deeds, the fruit; and in Shovavim one removes the stains left after teshuvah.
'Kedoshim tihyu' means, as the Ramban explains, to sanctify oneself in what is permitted and not be a glutton within the Torah's permission, and it was said to all of Klal Yisroel.

Chanoch, who withdrew and became an angel but neglected his generation, embodies 'Hashem'; Avraham, who went down to the lowest people, embodies 'Elokeichem'; 'kedoshim tihyu' asks for holiness that does not contradict closeness to people.
Nissan is the birth of creation and Tishrei its bar mitzvah; Rabbi Eliezer, a man of din, holds the world was created in Tishrei, and Rabbi Yehoshua, of Beis Hillel's chesed, in Nissan.
The first se'ir of Rosh Chodesh was burned not as a failure but as the best sign: on the day of the Mishkan the moon was whole, so the atonement for its lessening was not needed.

Nadav and Avihu entered after drinking wine because they already felt the time of Eliyahu, when the Gemara says one will be able to make wine a fixed meal and wine will no longer harm; it was a sign of their greatness.

Yayin (70) is the Name of Hashem (26) plus dam (44): a little wine, used for kedushah, is the Name, while too much leaves only blood; this is why Kiddush begins 'Yom hashishi vayechulu', whose initials spell the Name.

Keeping Shabbos Shuvah, as testimony to creation, makes a Jew a partner in Hashem's creation of the new year.
Why are these days called the Day of Judgment, when the brachos of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur speak only of Hashem's kingship?
How can one say the world gets better each year when the streets and even the shuls seem to show decline?
If a person passed last year's judgment and is no worse now, why should he not pass again?
How can a person be compelled until he says he wants to bring the korban, when it must be his own will?
The Rav says every Jew should make a cheshbon to improve himself over last year so that he fits into the new, better year.

The Rav calls for a Shabbos Shuvah like never before: a cheshbon hanefesh on how to improve one's Shabbos, feeling oneself a witness to creation, and extra care in its laws, including the rabbinic ones and muktzeh.
The Rav says one should keep Shabbos with joy so that Hashem too has oneg and nachas from His children.
The Rav says that on Yom Kippur each Jew should dig into his heart until he consciously reaches the point that wants to do Hashem's will.
The Rav asks that people daven for Klal Yisrael and for every need, and that all Jews do teshuvah and improve together with the new world.

Adar, the last month and a time of hester panim, has its salvation in its very lowness: one who has fallen to the bottom must rise.
According to the Ramban on Haazinu, the geulah is promised unconditionally, not dependent on teshuvah, and is the one part of the shirah still waiting to be fulfilled.
The tekufah of Teves, the longest and darkest night, became a festival of avodah zarah, and this is the source of the custom not to learn Torah on Nittel.
Teves is the hardest month because it begins the last degel, of Dan, and a beginning carries in it the strength of the whole.
Jews of the final, darkest galus are, according to the Rav, the most precious to Hashem, as Hashem called Yaakov twice by name when he went down to galus at night.
The danger of Asarah b'Teves is nearness, 'samach', to the king of Bavel, and the remedy is nearness to a tzaddik, as Yehudah felt kedushah when he came close to Yosef.

A beginning holds the strength of the whole: just as the first day of Sefirah already carries the fiftieth day, so Teves, opening the last degel, carries the full weight of the end, while Adar, at rock bottom, must rise.
Since everything foretold in Haazinu, all the troubles of galus, has already come true, the one missing part, the geulah, is certain, and it does not depend on teshuvah.
Using the Sefer Yetzirah's parallel of space, time and soul, the Rav explains that just as there are places where the Torah forbids learning, there must be a time, and that is Nittel.
The Jews of the last galus are the most precious to Hashem because their night is so dark that even a small act of avodah, like a hurried Minchah, is precious to Him.

The word 'samach' teaches that mere nearness to a rasha lets his tumah in even before any wall is breached, and the same power works for good when one is near a tzaddik, as Yehudah felt kedushah near Yosef.

Each of the twelve months is a different arrangement of the four letters of the Shem Havaya.
The Yud and Vav are masculine and chesed, the Heis feminine and din; when the masculine comes first, chesed sweetens din.
Tammuz and Teves are reversed arrangements of din, and their din spills into Av and Shevat until the fifteenth of the month.
From Tu B'Shvat until Shavuos the gates of chesed are open, and these days are meant to be used for Torah and avodah.
Seraf (580) rising into the ilan (91) shows the power of tumah being raised and absorbed into kedushah.
On Tu B'Shvat one davens for the esrog, and the berachah on fruit is said with the 'pri etz hadar' in mind.
The order of the letters decides which middah rules: masculine first means chesed sweetens din, feminine first means din dominates, which is why Esav put his wives before his sons.
Writing right to left follows the Aleph-Beis order of chesed: Esav writes the other way, while the descendants of Avraham also write from right to left.
Tu B'Shvat falls on the fifteenth because the din of Teves overlaps into the first half of Shevat, just as the din of Tammuz lasts in Av until Chamishah Asar B'Av.
Seraf equals 580, the numerical value of the two names of tumah and of Seir, and ilan equals 91, Havaya and Adnus together; the sap rising in the tree is tumah being raised into kedushah.
The roshei teivos of the passuk for Nissan read in the Aleph-Beis order, while the arrangement of Tammuz and Teves comes from sofei teivos, the Aleph-Beis backwards.
In the borei pri ha'etz of Tu B'Shvat lies a remez to the pri etz hadar, the esrog, and the great success of Klal Yisrael comes through the four minim.

The Rav says the days from Tu B'Shvat to Shavuos should be used for Torah and avodah, drawing down chesed while the gates are open.
The Rav says that when making borei pri ha'etz on Tu B'Shvat one has in mind the pri etz hadar, the esrog.
The Rav does not advocate changing accepted etiquette, but asks that one not criticize those who keep the order of kedushah.

Pesach is the beginning of the bond between Hashem and Klal Yisrael, lesser than the later Yamim Tovim, yet its chametz prohibition carries kares because eating matzah binds a Jew to Hashem.
Pesach is the reishis that contains everything and a time of renewal, mirrored in the reawakening of nature in Nisan.
Bread contains the ten utterances of creation and therefore satisfies every kind of person, but its holiness is received only when one eats as a Jew should.
Matzah, equal to three times the full spelling of Hashem's Name, comes from a higher source than bread and is the key that opens a world beyond grasp.
On Pesach every Jew goes through a rebirth, and Hashem knocks on the door and asks Klal Yisrael to open up to Him.
Each Yom Tov has its gift; the gift of Pesach is geulah, and only one who wants it receives it.
The Rav reads kares and kashrus as opposites: just as eating chametz on Pesach cuts the bond with Hashem, eating matzah ties it, a level of connection no other Yom Tov's mitzvah reaches.

The spring that reawakens nature in Nisan is the earthly reflection of the joy in Heaven over the new bond with Klal Yisrael, the song of the Chassan and Kallah that Shlomo HaMelech put into Shir Hashirim.

Bread equals three times the Name of Hashem (78), while matzah equals three times its full spelling, 'Mah' (135): matzah draws from a holiness so high it can only be asked about, which is why the Seder begins with questions.
The matzah is the key of birth that Hashem keeps for Himself, and the Targum calls matzah 'patira', an opening, like 'peter rechem'.

Following the Ba'al HaTanya, the matzah's flour and water are only a capsule; inside is the same light of Yetzias Mitzrayim that the Jews ate in Mitzrayim, so the matzah is the original and not a copy.
The tal of 'my head is filled with dew' is the first three letters of the Name in full spelling (39), which descends to the final hei, Klal Yisrael, and that is the matzah.
If Pesach is the lesser beginning, why is its prohibition of chametz punished with kares, unlike the prohibitions of Shavuos and Sukkos?
Why does every person need variety in food yet never tire of bread?
Why is the Seder opened with a child asking?
How can we say of our matzah 'this is the bread our fathers ate in Mitzrayim', when that matzah was eaten long ago?

The Rav says Pesach is a time for every Jew to make a reckoning and become a new person, throwing off the shrouds of the yetzer hara and aveiros.
The Rav says one should approach the table with proper holiness and eat as a Jew is supposed to eat, with a bracha and preparation, not like Esav.
The Rav says that on this day one should daven that Hashem alone be King and that Mashiach be His chariot.
The Rav says that just as Hashem shows Himself in completeness on Yom Tov, a Jew should prepare and present himself to Hashem in completeness.
The Rav says a Jew should develop a desire for geulah, to be freed from the yetzer hara, and not pass Yom Tov nonchalantly.

A tzaddik who learns Torah lishmah raises himself until his name is Torah, so the Mishnah names him and mentioning his name is like saying words of Torah.
A tzaddik's name, and even the name of the place where he lived, carries his kedushah and can draw down a yeshuah for the one who mentions it.
The reward of one who learns Torah lishmah is so great that not even a navi saw it, and the whole world is worthwhile for him alone.
Everything that happens in the world, great or small, happens for the sake of the tzaddikim and Klal Yisrael, even when nobody knows why.
Mitzvos rise to Heaven and come down as blessing, aveiros come down as suffering, and the greatest blessing comes from Torah lishmah.
The one who learns lishmah has no interest of his own, so he loves Hashem and people alike and is loved by both.
The Torah he learns keeps him far from sin: Hashem gives such tzaddikim a special sense that warns them away from forbidden food.
The Mishnah names its Tannaim not only to know who said what: a tzaddik who learns lishmah becomes so holy that his very name is Torah, so saying 'Rabbi Akiva' is like saying a word of Torah.

A name in loshon hakodesh is the creature's essence: Adam saw from each animal's nature which letters it was made of, and a sinner loses his name, which is why Zimri and Cozbi are named only after Pinchas killed them.
The holier a thing is, the more easily it is spoiled; wine, which stands for the reward of Olam Haba, is spoiled even by a gentile's look, showing how holy that reward is.
World events like Vashti's death or Nixon's resignation are reported with worldly reasons, but their true cause is the tzaddikim and Klal Yisrael, which will become clear only when Mashiach comes.
The heavenly calls to teshuvah go out every day, and the receiver that picks them up is a Jewish heart; a sudden urge to do teshuvah is the heart catching one of them.
Machlokes comes from each person's private interests; one who learns lishmah has none, which is why he can love everyone, as all will in the days of Mashiach.
Loving a fellow Jew does not divide one's love of Hashem, since every Jew's neshamah is a part of Hashem; this is why 'love your fellow as yourself' ends with 'I am Hashem'.
